reviewers.summary: The headline conclusion is invalidated by deterministic enrollment-order allocation and an uncorrected marginal result selected from six unregistered outcomes. Participant totals, effect-size reporting, and the claimed relative improvement are also internally inconsistent, while the proposed sleep mechanism, clinical significance, population generalisation, workplace recommendation, and reproducibility claims exceed the supplied evidence.
suggested_improvements: Run a preregistered, adequately powered study with randomized allocation, concealment, blinded outcome scoring, and a credible control condition.
Designate one primary endpoint and analysis in advance, adjust secondary-outcome inference for multiplicity, and report effect sizes with confidence intervals.
Use objective sleep-duration or sleep-architecture measurements and a prespecified mediation analysis before advancing a sleep-restriction mechanism.
Recruit participants outside the authors' laboratory across a population relevant to the intended workplace claim.
Deposit de-identified data, task materials, analysis code, spreadsheet formulas, and calibrated spectral and timing parameters in a persistent repository.

reviewers.detail: reviewer did not return the required JSON schema

reviewers.summary: The manuscript reports a single borderline-significant result (p=0.047) from an n=12 study with non-random, enrollment-order-based group assignment, no correction across six comparisons, a mislabeled small effect size called 'large', and causal/generalizing language that exceeds what the design and data support; several internal inconsistencies (e.g., 14% vs cited 3-5% improvement) and an unsupported mechanistic claim from a non-significant sleep-quality result further weaken the conclusions.
suggested_improvements: Randomize (or otherwise conceal) group allocation instead of using enrollment order.
Report effect sizes with confidence intervals for all six outcomes, not just the significant one.
Conduct an a priori power analysis; n=12 is likely underpowered to detect d≈0.3 reliably.
Preregister hypotheses and analysis plan, and deposit raw data/code in an open repository.
State the manufacturer-supplied LED panel as a potential conflict of interest more prominently, not only in the funding line.

reviewers.summary: This n=12 sequential (non-randomised) lab-student study cannot support the causal, clinical, or workplace claims in the title and Discussion: the sole p=0.047 2-back contrast is one of six uncorrected tests, Cohen's d=0.31 both contradicts t(10)=2.27 and is not a large effect, 9 women plus 4 men do not sum to n=12, the advertised 14% relative gain is about 8.5% and is not consistent with 3–5% morning-light figures, and a p=0.08 sleep difference is narrated as a memory-consolidation mechanism. Reject pending a randomised, multiplicity-controlled, openly reported design whose claims match the evidence.
suggested_improvements: Re-analyse with one preregistered primary endpoint (2-back) and treat the other five tasks as exploratory, reporting 95% CIs and TOST equivalence tests on the nulls instead of six uncorrected p-values.

Replace sequential enrollment with a counterbalanced within-subject crossover whose control arm is matched on melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance, not photopic lux, so hue is not confounded with circadian drive.
Deposit trial-level accuracy, the spreadsheet formulae, and manufacturer spectral power distributions in an open repository rather than 'on reasonable request'.

Inventive follow-up: run n-of-1 sequential Bayesian sessions in which a wearable melanopic dosimeter times the LED to each person's dim-light melatonin onset and stops when that individual's posterior on next-day 2-back excludes a prespecified MCID, publishing a 'circadian passport' of personal light-timing posteriors instead of a single underpowered group t-test.

findings.issue: The sentence “Because the measures address distinct cognitive domains, no correction for multiple comparisons was applied” leaves the sole positive result, “t(10) = 2.27, p = 0.047,” unsupported after accounting for six tested outcomes.
findings.rationale: No primary outcome was preregistered, six hypotheses were tested, and only the marginal result was highlighted; a Bonferroni threshold is 0.05/6 = 0.0083, so p = 0.047 does not support the headline conclusion.

findings.issue: The sentence “the first six enrollees formed the blue-light group and the remaining six the control group” makes the later claim that exposure “causes a clinically meaningful improvement” invalid because treatment is perfectly confounded with enrollment order.
findings.rationale: Any systematic difference between early and late enrollees can produce the observed group difference, and the post-test-only design provides no baseline measurement with which to assess that confounding.
findings.test_suggestion: Compare baseline and enrollment-order covariates for positions 1–6 versus 7–12; condition is perfectly collinear with that split, so its independent causal effect is unidentifiable.

findings.issue: "the first six enrollees formed the blue-light group and the remaining six the control group" — assignment was by enrollment order, not randomized.
findings.rationale: Order-of-enrollment assignment confounds group membership with time, motivation, or scheduling effects, undermining any causal interpretation of the group difference.
findings.test_suggestion: Re-analyze with randomized allocation or include enrollment-order/time as a covariate; check whether the effect survives.

findings.issue: "The effect size (Cohen's d = 0.31) indicates a large effect."
findings.rationale: By standard convention d≈0.3 is a small-to-medium effect, not large; mislabeling it inflates the apparent strength of the headline finding.
findings.test_suggestion: assert classify_cohens_d(0.31) == 'small' (Cohen 1988 thresholds: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large)

findings.issue: "These results demonstrate that a single hour of evening blue-light exposure causes a clinically meaningful improvement in working memory in adults."
findings.rationale: With n=12, non-random group assignment, and one borderline p=0.047 result among six uncorrected tests, causal, generalized language is not supported by the evidence.

findings.issue: "Group differences on each of the six outcome measures were tested with independent-samples t-tests (two-tailed, alpha = 0.05). Because the measures address distinct cognitive domains, no correction for multiple comparisons was applied," and the only 'significant' result is "t(10) = 2.27, p = 0.047".
findings.rationale: Six uncorrected 0.05 tests make a single p = 0.047 expected under a weak null; Bonferroni α = 0.05/6 ≈ 0.008 (or Holm/FDR) would render the 2-back contrast non-significant, so the title claim that blue light improves working memory is not statistically supported.

findings.issue: Assignment was "according to the order in which they enrolled: the first six enrollees formed the blue-light group and the remaining six the control group," yet Discussion states "These results demonstrate that a single hour of evening blue-light exposure causes a clinically meaningful improvement in working memory in adults."
findings.rationale: First-six versus last-six enrollment is not randomization; calendar time, lab events, and expectancy are aliased with treatment, so a causal and clinical claim is not licensed by the design.
findings.test_suggestion: Treat enrollment rank as a confound: if outcome ~ light + enrollment_order, the light coefficient is unidentified when light is a step function of order (first 6 vs last 6).

findings.issue: "The effect size (Cohen's d = 0.31) indicates a large effect" sits beside Results "t(10) = 2.27, p = 0.047" on two groups of six.
findings.rationale: Equal-n Cohen's d = t * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2) = 2.27 * sqrt(1/3) ≈ 1.31, so 0.31 contradicts the reported t; separately, d = 0.31 is small by Cohen's benchmarks (0.2/0.5/0.8), which undercuts "clinically meaningful" and "large".

findings.issue: The sentence “Twelve volunteers (n = 12; 9 women, 4 men; mean age 24.1 years)” reports sex-category counts summing to 13 rather than 12.
findings.rationale: This prevents verification of the sample composition and raises uncertainty about which reported sample size was used in the analysis.

findings.issue: The sentence “The effect size (Cohen's d = 0.31) indicates a large effect” is internally inconsistent because d = 0.31 is not conventionally large and cannot accompany t(10) = 2.27 with two groups of six.
findings.rationale: For an equal-size independent-samples t-test, d = t×sqrt(1/6+1/6), yielding approximately 1.31; therefore the reported t statistic, sample sizes, or effect size is erroneous, and the magnitude claim cannot be evaluated until corrected.
findings.test_suggestion:
from math import sqrt
d = 2.27 * sqrt(1/6 + 1/6)
assert abs(d - 0.31) < 0.01

findings.issue: The sentence “The 14% relative improvement we observed (81.3 vs 74.9)” miscalculates the relative increase, which is approximately 8.5%.
findings.rationale: The absolute increase is 6.4 percentage points, and 6.4/74.9×100 = 8.54%; the incorrect value materially exaggerates the reported benefit.

findings.issue: The sentence “Self-reported sleep quality was lower in the blue-light group (p = 0.08), which we interpret as evidence that blue light consolidates memory through mild sleep restriction” infers a mechanism from a nonsignificant outcome that neither measures sleep restriction nor establishes mediation.
findings.rationale: At the prespecified alpha of 0.05, p = 0.08 is not evidence of a group difference; moreover, subjective sleep quality is not sleep duration, and no association or mediation analysis connects it to 2-back performance.

findings.issue: The sentences “These results demonstrate that a single hour of evening blue-light exposure causes a clinically meaningful improvement in working memory in adults” and “we recommend that blue-light panels be adopted in workplace wellness programmes” exceed evidence from twelve graduate students in one laboratory and an unvalidated task-accuracy difference.
findings.rationale: The narrow convenience sample cannot establish effects across adults or workplace populations, no clinical-meaningfulness threshold or confidence interval is supplied, and the study provides no evidence about workplace benefits or harms.
findings.test_suggestion: Attempt to identify a prespecified clinical threshold, its confidence interval, and a representative workplace sampling frame; none is reported.

findings.issue: The sentence “Analyses were performed in a spreadsheet; the raw data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request” does not provide the task implementations, scoring rules, descriptive statistics, spreadsheet formulas, device calibration, or accessible data needed to reproduce the result.
findings.rationale: An independent researcher cannot recreate the intervention or six outcomes, audit the contradictory t and d values, or rerun the analysis from the information supplied.
findings.test_suggestion: Give the excerpt and cited materials to an independent analyst and require exact reconstruction of the six measures and reported t statistic without contacting the authors.

findings.issue: "The 14% relative improvement we observed (81.3 vs 74.9) is consistent with prior reports of 3-5% improvements from morning light."
findings.rationale: A 14% change is not consistent with a cited 3-5% range; this internal inconsistency overstates agreement with prior literature.

findings.issue: "Because the measures address distinct cognitive domains, no correction for multiple comparisons was applied."
findings.rationale: Six uncorrected tests substantially raise the chance that the single p=0.047 result on the 2-back task is a false positive.
findings.test_suggestion: Apply Bonferroni/Holm correction (alpha/6 ≈ 0.0083) to the six p-values and check if p=0.047 remains significant.

findings.issue: "Self-reported sleep quality was lower in the blue-light group (p = 0.08), which we interpret as evidence that blue light consolidates memory through mild sleep restriction."
findings.rationale: p=0.08 is non-significant by the paper's own alpha=0.05 threshold, yet is used to assert a specific causal mechanism not supported by the data.

findings.issue: "All participants were graduate students in the same department" recruited "from the authors' laboratory group."
findings.rationale: A homogeneous convenience sample cannot support the general claim of improvement 'in adults' made in the title and Discussion.

findings.issue: The sentence "Twelve volunteers (n = 12; 9 women, 4 men; mean age 24.1 years)" gives a sex breakdown that sums to 13, not 12.
findings.rationale: Headline n, t(10), and the demographic split cannot all be true; until the sample composition is reconciled, every subsequent percentage and test is on an undefined denominator.

findings.issue: "The 14% relative improvement we observed (81.3 vs 74.9) is consistent with prior reports of 3-5% improvements from morning light."
findings.rationale: (81.3 - 74.9) / 74.9 ≈ 8.5%, not 14%, and neither 14% nor 8.5% is numerically consistent with a 3–5% morning-light literature figure; the comparison also mixes evening with morning exposure.

findings.issue: "Self-reported sleep quality was lower in the blue-light group (p = 0.08), which we interpret as evidence that blue light consolidates memory through mild sleep restriction."
findings.rationale: p = 0.08 is not a demonstrated effect, there is no mediation test, and worse sleep is not shown to cause better 2-back scores; the mechanism therefore exceeds the evidence (correlation/non-significance read as causation).
findings.test_suggestion: assert 0.08 < 0.05  # fails; no indirect-effect CI is reported either

findings.issue: From "Twelve volunteers... recruited from the authors' laboratory group. All participants were graduate students in the same department," the paper concludes an effect "in adults" and "recommend[s] that blue-light panels be adopted in workplace wellness programmes".
findings.rationale: A convenience n = 12 of in-lab graduate students (mean age 24.1) is not the adult or worker population named in the title and policy recommendation.
findings.test_suggestion: Population claimed ('adults'/'workplace') vs sampled ('authors' laboratory group' graduate students): no sampling frame or eligibility beyond the lab is specified.

findings.issue: "Analyses were performed in a spreadsheet; the raw data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request," with "Preregistration: none" and control specified only as "room light, 300 lux".
findings.rationale: No script, no open data, no preregistered analysis path, and no control spectrum or melanopic EDI means an independent team cannot repeat the lighting or the statistics.
findings.test_suggestion: Attempt to recreate the t(10)=2.27 result from deposited raw scores and a stated control SPD; neither is provided.

findings.issue: "Because the 2-back task is the gold-standard measure of executive function, we recommend that blue-light panels be adopted in workplace wellness programmes."
findings.rationale: Overstating the task's epistemic status to justify a policy recommendation from one small, underpowered study is unwarranted.

findings.issue: "the raw data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request" and "Preregistration: none."
findings.rationale: Absence of preregistration, open data, and shared analysis code limits independent verification of the reported effect.

findings.issue: "Because the 2-back task is the gold-standard measure of executive function, we recommend that blue-light panels be adopted in workplace wellness programmes pending replication."
findings.rationale: The 2-back indexes working-memory updating, not a consensus gold standard of executive function as a whole; that over-label is then used to justify a workplace recommendation.

required_next_actions: Reproduce each of the 23 CRITICAL/WARNING finding(s) with a failing test before authoring any fix.
Triage all 14 suggested_improvements — apply-and-verify or reject with a reason. None may be silently dropped.
Append one JSONL line per ruling to .ensemble_reviews/dispositions.jsonl with run_id rev_20260904131823_wvxh, then present the disposition table.

decision_rule: Consensus prioritizes investigation; the governor must reproduce and verify before editing.
